uncited: Primitive Geometry and Distribution defines the mathematical representation of individual splats (primitives) in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifying how position, orientation, scale, and density are parameterized and projected.
It solves the problem of representing complex 3D scenes with a set of differentiable, analytically tractable basis functions that can be efficiently rasterized.

It sets itself apart from its siblings by establishing the baseline 3D Gaussian ellipsoid model, whereas alternatives modify the distribution shape (e.g., Student's t, Generalized Exponential), dimensionality (2D disks), or conditioning (Direct Gaussian Splatting) to address specific limitations like geometry accuracy or computational cost.

The family shares the core mechanism of representing a scene as a collection of $N$ independent primitives, each defined by a mean position $\boldsymbol{\mu}$, a covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, and an opacity $\alpha$.
The rendering process relies on projecting these 3D distributions into 2D screen space and alpha-compositing them.
**Mean Position** ($\boldsymbol{\mu}_i$): A 3D vector $(x, y, z)$ in world space.
To render, the 3D covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i$ is projected to 2D screen space.
Let $\mathbf{W}$ be the view rotation matrix and $\mathbf{J}$ be the Jacobian of the projective transformation.
The effective opacity at the pixel is $\alpha_i T_i(u)$.
It emerged as a real-time alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), leveraging the efficiency of rasterization while maintaining high-fidelity rendering.
The method builds on the concept of volumetric rendering but replaces the implicit neural network with explicit, differentiable Gaussian primitives.

The family of variants described here has developed to address specific weaknesses of the original Gaussian ellipsoid, such as poor geometry representation (leading to 2DGS and LinPrim), limited expressivity for sharp features (leading to GES and SSS), and computational overhead in conditioning (leading to dGS).
